analysis.one_liner: Expands federal enforcement, funding, and penalties against copyright piracy and counterfeit goods.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2007 with a Democratic sponsor and Republican cosponsors, and its committee held hearings, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would build a larger federal enforcement machine for intellectual property: an FBI unit of at least 10 agents dedicated to IP crimes, extra FBI agents in computer-crime units, annual agent training, federal prosecutors posted in Hong Kong and Budapest, and a task force targeting organized piracy. It would let the Attorney General sue suspected copyright infringers in civil court instead of prosecuting them, add forfeiture of property and restitution in copyright cases, ban exporting pirated copies as well as importing them, and stiffen penalties for trafficking in counterfeit goods and recording movies in theaters. It authorizes roughly $32 million a year through 2011 for FBI and Justice Department work.
analysis.who_benefits: Large copyright and trademark holders — movie studios, record labels, software publishers, and brand owners — gain a taxpayer-funded enforcement arm that investigates and sues on their behalf, plus forfeiture, restitution, and tougher penalties. The Attorney General also gains a new civil route to penalize suspected infringers. Consumers get some secondary benefit from crackdowns on counterfeit goods.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Movie studios, record labels, software and brand owners

how_it_helps.text: Creates an FBI operational unit of at least 10 agents to investigate complex, multi-district, and international intellectual property crimes, and assigns additional FBI agents to Justice Department computer-crime units [S2] [S3].

Assigns a federal prosecutor to the Justice Department office in Hong Kong and one in Budapest to coordinate international IP enforcement, and creates a task force targeting organized crime syndicates involved in IP theft [S2] [S3].

Authorizes $12 million per year through fiscal 2011 for the IP enforcement program, plus $10 million per year each to the FBI and the Justice Department's Criminal Division for computer-crime investigators and forensic tools [S3].
Lets the Attorney General bring a civil action for copyright infringement in place of a criminal case, with penalties and restitution flowing to the copyright owner [S2] [S3].

Adds civil and criminal forfeiture of property used in or derived from IP crimes, requires restitution to victims, and enhances penalties for trafficking in counterfeit labels, goods, and pirated recordings [S2] [S3].
Bans exportation of infringing copies as well as importation, closing off the cross-border movement of pirated goods [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new FBI units, overseas prosecutors, and task force — about $32 million a year — largely to enforce private copyright and trademark rights. People accused of infringement face broader civil penalties, property forfeiture, and stiffer criminal exposure, and the definition of 'financial gain' expands to cover receiving other copyrighted works, reaching some noncommercial sharing. People moving lawfully bought media across borders face new restrictions because exportation, not just importation, becomes infringement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and people accused of infringement

drawbacks.text: The public pays for enforcement that mainly protects private rights-holders' revenue: the bill authorizes $12 million a year for the IP enforcement program plus $10 million each year to the FBI and $10 million to the Justice Department's Criminal Division through fiscal 2011 [S3].

Forfeiture is broad: it covers 'any property used, or intended to be used, in any manner or part' to commit or facilitate an IP offense, and proceeds derived from it, with procedures borrowed from federal drug forfeiture law [S3].

The bill expands what counts as criminal 'financial gain' to include receipt of other copyrighted works, and adds a 'traffic in' definition covering possession with intent to distribute — language that reaches beyond large-scale commercial pirates [S3].

Making exportation of infringing copies an infringement applies to copies leaving the United States, which can sweep in individuals moving media and recordings across borders, not just trafficking networks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Cracking down on commercial counterfeiting and organized piracy has real public value — counterfeit goods can be unsafe and the trade funds criminal networks. But the bill's design puts the costs on taxpayers and broadens legal exposure for ordinary conduct (forfeiture of any 'facilitating' property, sharing counted as financial gain, export bans), while the main beneficiaries are large studios, labels, software firms, and brand owners. It is an enforcement expansion written for the interests of rights-holders first.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2007 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held a hearing but never reported or voted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Senator Patrick Leahy introduced the bill on November 7, 2007, for himself and Senator John Cornyn, giving it sponsorship from both parties [S1] [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and the committee held hearings on the measure [S5].
No further action — no committee vote, no floor vote — was recorded before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5] [S1].
The bill attracted two Republican cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers are better off because roughly $32 million a year was never appropriated for enforcement of private copyright claims, and people who trade unauthorized copies avoid the bill's expanded penalties and property forfeiture. Copyright and trademark industries did not get the new enforcement machinery they sought.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill with a Republican as original cosponsor and two Republicans cosponsoring in total, but no vote ever took place, so whether support or opposition split by party was never tested [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Movie studios, record labels, and software publishers
industries.note: They would gain a dedicated FBI unit, overseas prosecutors, civil actions brought by the Attorney General, forfeiture, and restitution — enforcement of their private copyrights financed by taxpayers. Broader criminal definitions and export restrictions also reach ordinary people who share or move media, keeping cheaper copies and gray-market goods off the market.

industries.industry: Brand owners and retailers of trademarked goods
industries.note: Enhanced penalties for trafficking in counterfeit goods and packaging, plus forfeiture and destruction of counterfeits, protect consumers from unsafe fake products as well as brand revenue.

industries.industry: Gray-market importers and resellers of media
industries.note: The bill makes exporting infringing copies an infringement alongside importation and applies the restrictions to goods departing the United States, narrowing the cross-border resale trade in cheaper genuine and copied media.

The FBI and Justice Department gain new units, training programs, overseas positions, and about $32 million a year in authorized funding through fiscal 2011, expanding their reach into intellectual property cases.
